claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a homogeneous, single-phase BCC alloy at high temperature.
The range of phases formed during cooling and thermal exposure is primarily caused by diffusional segregation of Al during slow cooling.
Al diffuses faster than Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni under the relevant cooling conditions.
Slow cooling permits local Al enrichment and depletion within the BCC matrix.
Longer residence in a critical temperature interval can affect phase nucleation.
Changing cooling rate can alter phase composition in an Al-containing Co-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloy.
Local compositional fluctuations alter the chemical environment and lower the nucleation barrier for secondary phases.
Al-enriched or Al-depleted regions facilitate formation of FCC or ordered-BCC phases during cooling or subsequent aging.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion and preserves a homogeneous BCC structure with minimal Al segregation.
After identical aging, slowly cooled samples will contain a greater fraction of secondary phases than rapidly quenched samples.
The secondary phases in slowly cooled samples will be detectable by diffraction and microscopy.
Local Al-content variations will spatially correlate with newly formed secondary phases.
The proposed diffusion-mediated mechanism should dominate only at cooling rates slow enough to permit significant atomic migration.
Under ultra-rapid quenching, the alloy should remain in a metastable BCC state because diffusion is suppressed.
No statistically significant increase in either Al segregation or secondary-phase fraction after slow cooling would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Formation of the same phases regardless of cooling rate would falsify the proposed cooling-rate-dependent mechanism.
